title: Why Can't Spain Get Gibraltar Back?

minor: 'the one piece of this map Spain says it never gave away' slightly overstates: Spain also disputes the waters, and the source only says the isthmus was never ceded. Suggest 'the piece of land Spain says it never ceded'.

'Spain said ending that status meant handing the land back; Britain said it meant letting the people choose' (1946-67 shot) has no listed source. It is a fair summary of the two positions, but add one.
'Spanish and British patrol boats often meet': the source says vessels meet and each government protests; 'often' is not documented, and 'vessels' is closer.
'Every working day, money crosses the gate both ways: wages go north, shoppers and supplies come south' has no source entry. It is plausible but not documented in the list.
'a yes vote from the people of Gibraltar': the source (2006 Constitution preamble) records a promise of consent, not specifically a referendum. 'the consent of Gibraltar's people' is safer.
The 2012 census is described as 'last full census'. The source says so, but confirm no later census has been published before release, since the figure is repeated in the outro.
The Spanish and French 'siege lines vanish' and 'besieging lines pull back' are visual metaphors, not events. They are fine as map actions.

The outro's causal sentence 'Spain can't get Gibraltar back because the Rock is no longer only a line in a treaty' is the video's editorial conclusion, not a documented fact. It is acceptable as the thesis but should stay framed as the answer the video argues.

Gibraltar sits where Spain's south coast almost touches Africa.
It is a narrow peninsula about five kilometres long, tied to Spain by a flat strip of sand.
Most of it is one limestone ridge, the Rock, with sheer cliffs dropping into the sea on its eastern side.

Britain keeps a naval base on the Rock, where its warships and submarines can call at the mouth of the strait.
Now look north, at the flat strip of land where Gibraltar meets Spain.
Gibraltar had no flat ground to spare, so its airport runway was laid right across this strip.

shots.vo: In 1700 the King of Spain died without a child, and Europe went to war over his throne.
On 4 August 1704, an English and Dutch fleet took Gibraltar in the name of a rival claimant.
The small garrison surrendered after a short bombardment, and most Spanish residents chose to leave.
Many settled about eight kilometres north in San Roque, whose official title still says Gibraltar's city lives on there.
Nine years later, Britain and Spain made peace in the Dutch city of Utrecht, on 13 July 1713.
In Article X, Spain gave Britain the town, castle, port and forts of Gibraltar, to hold for ever.

shots.vo: So the first line was drawn around the town and its forts; Spain reads nothing beyond them as handed over.
Spain tried to take it back by force in 1727, and the siege failed within months.

shots.vo: Spain's besieging lines pull back, and the Rock's border stays drawn around the town and its forts.
Spain then built a fortified line across the isthmus, leaving a strip of neutral ground between the two sides.
Its biggest attempt was the Great Siege, when Spanish forces, joined later by French ones, surrounded the Rock.

The siege failed, and the peace treaty of 1783 left Gibraltar British once again.
The Spanish and French siege lines vanish from the isthmus; the British flag stays on the Rock.
In 1815, during a yellow fever outbreak, Britain set up camps on the neutral ground; Spain says only for a while.

shots.vo: Phone lines were cut and the ferry from Algeciras stopped, and the gate became a wall.
People on foot could cross again from December 1982; the border fully reopened in February 1985.
In 1986 Spain joined the European Community, today's EU, which Gibraltar had joined with Britain in 1973.
For thirty years the gate mattered less, until one vote in 2016 put it back at the centre of the map.
On 23 June 2016 the UK voted to leave the EU; Gibraltar voted 19,322 to 823 to stay.
Overnight, the gate at La Línea became a future outer border of the European Union.
In April 2017, EU leaders agreed that no EU-UK deal would cover Gibraltar without Spain's consent.

187 voted yes, and 17,900 voted no: about 99 percent of valid votes rejected it.
Gibraltar's government says the UN Charter's right of peoples to choose their own future outweighs a treaty from 1713.

shots.vo: It also points about 25 kilometres south, to Ceuta, a Spanish city on the coast of Africa.
Morocco says Ceuta and Melilla should be Moroccan; Spain says both are full and equal parts of Spain.
Both were Portuguese or Spanish long before 1704, and neither is on the UN's list.
Every working day, money crosses the gate both ways: wages go north into Spain, shoppers and supplies come south.
For the Spanish towns around the bay, La Línea, San Roque and Algeciras, that gate is a question of jobs.
So who should decide what a place is: the treaty that made it, or the people living there now?
By December 2020, Brexit's final deadline was days away, with no deal yet for the Rock's gate.
On 31 December 2020, hours before Brexit's transition ended, Spain and Britain agreed an outline for Gibraltar.

shots.vo: On 11 June 2025, in Brussels, the UK, Spain and the EU announced a political deal; a legal treaty had to follow.
Scenario one: the treaty takes effect, and routine checks at the land gate are removed.
Gibraltar would enter a customs union with the EU, so goods cross freely, and bring tobacco taxes closer to Spain's.
Passport checks for the EU's free-travel Schengen zone would move to Gibraltar's port and airport, with Spanish officers involved.
Both sides said the deal leaves their claims to sovereignty exactly where they were.

Spain can't get Gibraltar back because the Rock is no longer only a line in a treaty.
